questions.q: On day 1 of the capstone your partner wants to start coding to save time. What is the risk?
options: The code will not pass the eval set
The panel will not let you use an AI coding assistant
You build for the problem you imagined, not the one the client actually has
There will be no time left for the hand-over pack
questions.why: Week 11 is about understanding the problem; most failed POCs build something clever for the wrong problem.

questions.q: On kick-off day, what should you ask the mock client for first?
options: The last three real cases, rather than a description of the process
A full description of how the process should work
Access to their production systems
A list of features they would like
questions.why: Real cases reveal the actual pain, which a general process description often hides.

questions.q: In the support ticket example, day 1 showed tickets sit unassigned for hours. How did that change the plan?
options: The pair kept reply drafting as the main goal
The pair chose the full agent option to fix everything
The pair dropped the eval set to save time
The success measure became time to first assignment, and reply drafting became a later step
questions.why: Discovery found the real pain, so the brief and success measure moved to match it.

questions.q: Midway through the build, the mock client asks for an extra feature and you agree. How should you handle the scope change?
options: Just build it, since the client asked
Write it down and get the client to agree to the change
Build it quietly and mention it at the panel
Refuse, since scope can never change
questions.why: Scope can change, but silent scope changes count against you.

questions.q: A pair plans to pick the most advanced agent option to impress the panel. Why is that a weak plan?
options: Agents are not allowed in the capstone
The rubric rewards fit, measurement and trust, not how advanced the technology is
The panel only scores the demo
Advanced options always fail the eval set
questions.why: There is no score for advanced technology; a simple, measured, trusted solution scores better.

questions.q: Which of these is a checkable acceptance criterion?
options: The classifier is accurate
Users are happy with the results
The solution handles most tickets well
On the agreed 60-ticket eval set, the category matches the label for at least the agreed share, and every low-confidence ticket goes to a person
questions.why: A criterion must be markable true or false without arguing.

questions.q: When should you agree the targets in the acceptance criteria with the client?
options: Before you build, so nobody suspects the targets were set to fit the results
After the first eval run, so the targets are realistic
At the panel, once the demo is done
Only if the client asks for targets
questions.why: Targets set after seeing results are not trusted.

questions.q: Your options paper compares two LLM designs that differ only in prompt wording. What should you change?
options: Add a third prompt wording to have three options
Remove the comparison table and just recommend one
Make the options genuinely different, and include a non-AI option when one is plausible
Keep it; small changes are easier to compare
questions.why: Real options differ in approach, and a rule or form sometimes solves most of the problem.

questions.q: Your brief lists everything in scope but nothing out of scope. Why does that matter later?
options: It does not matter if the in-scope list is detailed
The client will reject a brief without a cost estimate
It makes the brief longer than one page
The out-of-scope list prevents most later arguments and lets you politely say no to new requests
questions.why: An agreed out-of-scope list is what you point to when new requests arrive under pressure.

questions.q: You use an LLM to turn interview notes into a draft brief. It adds a plausible number for weekly ticket volume. What do you do?
options: Keep it, since it looks reasonable
Delete or replace it unless it traces to your notes, documents or data
Keep it but round it to a nicer number
Ask the LLM to double-check its own number
questions.why: The LLM is not a source of facts about the client; every claim must trace to evidence.

questions.q: How should you choose most of the cases for the evaluation sheet?
options: From the cases you know the solution handles
From the easiest cases, so the pass rate is stable
At random from the client's real sample, then add edge and out-of-scope cases from discovery
From synthetic cases the LLM generates
questions.why: Random real cases show how the solution does on cases you did not pick.

questions.q: Why include a few out-of-scope cases in the evaluation sheet?
options: To check the solution says no when it should, because answering everything is a risk
To raise the pass rate with easy cases
Because the template needs exactly three
To test how fast the solution responds
questions.why: A solution that answers everything is a risk, not a feature.

questions.q: A failure turns out to be a wrong label, not a wrong answer. What do you do?
options: Agree the change with the client and note it in the sheet
Quietly fix the label to raise the pass rate
Leave it as a failure and never touch labels
Delete the case from the sheet
questions.why: Labels change only with the client's agreement and a note, never quietly to lift the score.

questions.q: Your HR policy assistant gives free-text answers. How should you decide pass or fail?
options: Use exact string matching against the expected answer
Count it as a pass if the answer is long enough
Write a short checklist a person could apply, test it by hand, then optionally use a judge you spot-check
Ask the LLM if its own answer is correct
questions.why: Two correct answers can use different words, so a clear checklist rule is needed.

questions.q: You scored 27 of 30 cases. How should you present that number in the demo?
options: As a precise 90 percent accuracy guarantee
Say it finds the main failure types but is not enough for a precise accuracy figure
Leave it out, since 30 cases is too few to mention
Round it up to show confidence
questions.why: Thirty cases is enough to find failure types, not to claim a precise accuracy figure.

questions.q: What should the first minute of the ten-minute capstone demo cover?
options: The system architecture
The team's tech stack
The evaluation pass rate
The problem in the client's words and the baseline number
questions.why: Opening with the client's problem and baseline keeps the demo about their need.

questions.q: The panel asks a question you cannot answer yet. What is the best response?
options: Give a confident estimate to keep momentum
Change the subject to a part you know well
Say you do not know yet and explain how you would find out or measure it
Promise it will be fixed in the next version
questions.why: An honest answer with a plan to measure earns more trust than a confident guess.

questions.q: During your panel demo, the live API call fails. What should you do?
options: Debug it live until it works
Restart the demo from the beginning
Skip to questions and end early
Say so calmly, switch to the screen recording and carry on
questions.why: Panels care more about how you handle a failure than about the failure itself.

questions.q: How do you test that your hand-over pack really works before the panel?
options: Ask someone outside your pair to run the POC and the evaluation from the README alone
Have your partner read through it
Check that every section heading is filled in
Ask an LLM whether the README is clear
questions.why: If a person who was not in the pair can run it alone, someone else can support it.

questions.q: Which item belongs in the capstone hand-over pack?
options: The API key values for the next owner
The evaluation sheet and the latest results
A full log of every chat with your AI coding assistant
Your personal access tokens
questions.why: The pack includes the eval sheet and results; secrets are named and located, never included.
